May I say to my right hon. friend that if there is one thing which is needed in Canada to-day more than anything else it is a note of confidence and optimism, not the attitude of detraction and pessimism which my right hon. friend is so fond of taking.
Why were we not able to effect these economies sooner? First of all, there were the legacies which were inherited from the preceding government. There were legacies which grew out of their own extravagance. There were the legacies of war, the increase in the public debt resulting therefrom, the amount that has had to be paid in pensions, and for soldiers' civil re-establishment, and a large amount for soldier land settlement; and miscellaneous amounts involved in the refunding of the debt, an operation that relates particularly to the war bonds. Then, in addition there have been the special obligations which we inherited in the nature of subsidies to provinces and grants made to the provinces for highways, for agricultural instruction, for technical education, large loans for housing, in unemployment relief and several other contributions. There have been the outlays on railways and merchant marine. I would like to give the House just a few particulars in regard to these matters, and as my right hon. friend is fond of getting the exact figures, I will give them to him. For the fiscal year 1919-20 there were total disbursements of $785,869,611, including advances to railways of $45,000,000. The amount was considerably larger than that of any year of the war, but it was the year of demobilization and much of the expenditure has to be put down to that head. For the fiscal year 1920-21 the total disbursements were still as high as $528,283,199, much of it due to the waste and extravagance of my right hon. friend. For the fiscal year

However, let me give the facts, with regard to reductions in the service in so far as we have found it possible to make them. First let me point out this fact: in attempting to reduce the service the government has been handicapped to a certain degree by some of the work of the Civil Service Commission. That commission had adopted a form of detailed classification in the different departments which some of us think is responsible to a considerable degree for the numbers that are kept in the service at the present time. That is one of the handicaps we have had to contend with. Another handicap which we have had to contend with in the service, so far as the showing by expenditure is concerned, is the fact that every year there has to be added increases in salaries in the nature of statutory increases. There is nothing to be found in any statute in the nature of a statutory decrease. They are all automatic increases; so that even if we kept the service at the point at which we found it, it would be inevitable that the amount that would have to be paid would be considerably in excess of the figures of the previous year.
There was the further fact that when we came into office we found a serious condition of unemployment throughout the country. As hon. gentlemen know, we were obliged the first winter to vote nearly a million dollars to alleviate the condition created by unemployment. Look at the press of this city to-day; note some of the comments that are being made concerning the intention of the government still further to reduce the public service; you find an appeal being made to the government not to make this reduction because we will add to the unemployment in the city. That condition was very serious when we took office. We had to go about matters carefully, but we did proceed nevertheless. We started in some of the departments in a quiet way, and whenever we found it possible . to reduce the numbers, we did so. With what result? With the result that up to the end of last year, we had made a very considerable net reduction in the public service. In some departments it was inevitable that we should make increases. Hon. members will recall that amongst legislation which we introduced was a good deal providing for increased inspection in different branches of agriculture, the existing inspection services were very considerably expanded, others were added with the result that in the Department of Agriculture we added some 237. In the Department of Finance there were additions of something like 67 owing to the fact that there are increased new services there.

May I add a word in reference to the outstanding reason why the burden of taxation on the country is what it is to-day? It is because the country to-day is obliged to carry the whole capital cost of the war. That is a statement that I want to make here on the floor of parliament. I made it in Quebec shortly before leaving for the old country. I saw that it was challenged during my absence; but I wish to repeat it here on the floor of parliament, that it has been left to the government that has succeeded the governments of my right hon. friend to pay every cent of the capital cost of the war including demobilization. During the whole period of the war and the period of demobilization, those six years, not a single cent was raised from the tax-payers of this country

to meet the obligations of the war, if we take what was left for that purpose after the government had used what was raised for its own expenditures in other directions. That is a very serious situation, and I say that my light hon. friend and his friends were guilty of distinct negligence in the administration of the affairs of this country, that at a time when they were prepared to conscript men, to send them overseas to fight, they were not ready to get after the men who were making great fortunes out of the war.

My right hon. friend has asked me to establish what I am saying. Let me again make clear the statement that this country to-day and for years to come will have to bear the capital cost of the war in whole, not in part, because of the neglect of my hon. friends opposite to meet any of the capital cost of the war during the period of the war and the period of demobilization. Some statement was made in challenge of that by the former Minister of Finance. I have examined his figures pretty carefully and what do I find? I find he has put down to his account the amount that he raised to pay the interest on the cost of the war during the period that he was in office. A payment of interest on capital is a payment for the privilege of not having to meet the capital cost. It is not a payment of part of the capital cost. The other amounts were amounts used for current pensions ; but pensions are not part of the capital cost of the war; they are part of the current obligations growing out of it and extending through the after years. Whether or not I am correct is a matter of simple addition and subtraction. Take the total disbursements and subtract the total receipts. See whether the balance is in excess or less than the amount that was spent on war account. These are the figures and what do they show.

The real explanation of the cost of government to-day and of the need for taxation is the manner in which the governments of which my right hon. friend was a member managed the affairs of the country during the period of the war andi the period of demobilization which succeeded it,-the outrageous policy of government borrowing to finance the war. The whole cost of the war, and of demobilization was thrown over upon the men and women of to-day-including those who fought in the war and have returned, >and the relatives of those who lost their lives in the nation's service. We are now meeting the cost of the war, its entire cost. In strict accounting, not a dollar of it was met by either the Conservative or Unionist governments of Sir Robert Borden, or by the government of my right hon. friend.

Not only did the governments of the day finance the war by borrowed money; not only did they let war profiteers go all but scot free, but in their loans they made the bonds they sold exempt from taxation, so that to-day they carry no part of the cost of the war to those who were fortunate enough to secure them.
To make still clearer my contention that the whole capital cost of the war was passed on until after the war, and still remains as a charge upon the country in spite of the large sums which were collected and are still being collected in war taxes, I may perhaps be permitted to use an illustration the force of which may appeal to those of us who were not reared in the lap of luxury. Many of us in the past, some of us perhaps in the present, have been all too well acquainted with the phenomenon known as the mortgage. We know in our individual experience how we may pay and still pay and pay in interest charges on the thing without being able to make any impression on the principal sum. Even over so short a period as five or six years we may pay in interest from one-third to one-half of the principal of the mortgage without having reduced that principal by a single dollar. Now, that is just what has happened in our national affairs. The hundreds of millions which were
raised by former governments in war taxation all went to pay interest on the rapidly increasing debt and the current expense of pensioning and re-establishing our returning soldiers. In no single year of the late government's term of office after the war broke out, were the amounts raised in war taxation sufficient to do more than meet current interest on war debt and current charges for pensions and the re-establishment of returned soldiers. I have said before, and I repeat, that the whole capital cost of the war is still constituting a mortgage upon the whole national wealth of Canada. What this country has to-day on its back is a mortgage equal to the whole capital cost of the war; and that mortgage was left by the hon. member and his friends.

I repeat, the late government failed grievously in its duty during the war period in not making heavier demands upon the self-sacrifice of our people and raising additional taxation sufficient to meet during the war a fair proportion of the capital cost of the war, as was done, for example, in England. Whatever their reason may be, they failed to do it; they loaded the entire charge of the war on the shoulders of their successors, and now they talk glibly to us about our extravagance and taxation.

I have no
desire to delay the House unduly, but in view of the kind of propaganda to which the country has been subjected during the last year I think it would be to the advantage of all concerned to have the facts brought out in their true light. There are fortunately certain statistics which do tell the truth as to whether a country is prospering or not. We have the statistics of production and of trade, we have the statistics of transportation, and we have the statistics of employment and of business generally, also of public finance. Let my hon. friend take any one of these groups or take them all and he will find in every single division that there are irrefutable evidences of increased prosperity in this country during the past year, and that of a notable character. These are the facts which the country would do well to take to heart, because after all it is a good thing for a people to know when their country is prospering. There is nothing to be gained by belittling the country and making conditions out to be bad when as a matter of fact they are good and improving every day.
My hon. friend spoke this afternoon particularly of the record in agriculture. Fortunately, through the bounty of Providence, there has been a great record so far as the crops are concerned; indeed, it is the greatest in the history of Canada notwithstanding that the crop of last year was at that time also the greatest. Of agricultural crops for the

year 1923, wheat gave a total yield of 474,-
199,000	bushels as contrasted with 399,000,000 in the year previous. The yield in oats was
537.000.	000 as against 491,000,000; hay and clover 14,845,000 tons as against 14,062,000 tons. In Canada there is certainly an abundance of food for man and beast, and of the wheat crop of nearly 475,000,000 bushels over
263.000.	000 were marketed before the close of the year. That is a fact which the government is entitled to take some credit for. Providence undoubtedly gave a bountiful harvest, but it remained with the administration and others associated with it to see that the harvest was to some degree marketed in as profitable a way as possible. Never before in the history of Canada has as much grain been marketed up to the close of the year as was done last year. That was due in part to lowered transportation and other costs, the lowering of which was brought about in some measure at the instance of .the government. As my hon. friends know, it was this government that restored the Crowsnest pass rates on grain in the West. This government also-referred back to the Railway Commisssion the matter of rates on grain to the Pacific coast from Alberta. These reduced rates had a good deal to do with the extent to which crops were marketed at the time, and the prices that obtained. An interesting development is the extent to which the wheat crop was shipped this year in part through the port of Vancouver. In 1920 the shipments of wheat via Vancouver amounted to less than one million bushels. This year the shipments to January 31st total
27,800,000	bushels, and it is probable that in all there will have been shipped for the crop year, the very high total of 50,000,000 bushels via Vancouver. Indeed, Canada will this year, as last, take the first place amongst the world's wheat exporting countries. Take other branches of agriculture. My hon. friend referred to some agricultural figures this afternoon, and perhaps it is well that we should consider some further figures in this connection. For the year 1922 the total value of our agricultural production, that is for field crops, animal products, dairy products and miscellaneous items, was estimated at $1,419,937,000, whilst the capita! value or gross agricultural wealth of Canada was placed at $6,773,942,000. These figures shew the important place which the agricultural industry holds in our national life.
Let us take mining, in regard to which there has been a very distinct revival. The figures for 1923 show a mineral production of $214,102,000; those for 1922 show a production of $184,297,000; whilst in 1921 the production was $171,923,000. In reference to coal con-

I come now to the question of the foreign trade. The visible balance last year was largely in our favour, one of the results being the rehabilitation of our currency on foreign exchanges. In 1921 it took 111.6 cents to make an American dollar; last year we had reached the point where 101.9 cents sufficed.
The exports of Canadian produce for the calendar year 1923 were $1,014,734,000, an increase of 27 per cent in two years.
The imports for consumption increased from $799,478,000 in 1921 to $903,530,000 in
1923.
The visible balance of trade which in 1921 was in our favor by only $3,222,000 had in

c'.eased to $111,204,000 in 1923.
Not the least gratifying effect of our recent trade policy has been that under it our imports from the United Kingdom have increased from $123,150,000 in 1921 to $136,-
859,000	in 1922 and $154,492,000 in 1923. While the full effects of the extensions made in the British preference are not yet shown * for a full year-they came into effect only on May 12, 1923-it is evident that Canada has been effectively contributing to promote that revival of British industry which is so badly needed in the United Kingdom, and which in its turn will contribute to improve our export trade at a time when our market on the European continent is threatened by the disturbed political, economic and financial conditions there prevailing.
Then take transportation. The total earnings notably increased last year, notwithstanding a downward tendency of freight rates. Especially was this true on the Canadian National Railways.	The total
earnings of Canadian railways for the eleven months ended November 1923 were $429,-
409,000,	or an increase of 6.6 per cent over the corresponding period of the year before, which came to $402,808,000. Out of this total increase of $26,601,000, the Canadian National absorbed about $19,274,000. or over 72 per cent. This has made possible the highly satisfactory statement by Sir Henry Thornton to the effect that the net operating revenues of the Canadian National Railway system will reach $20,127,000 for 1923, as compared with about $2,480,000 for 1922.
That the improved showing of the railways in 1923 is not merely on their financial side, but extends also to the physical volume of their traffic, is shown by the fact that the estimated tonnage of freight hauled in 1923 was 113,500,000 tons, as compared with 108,-
530,000	tons in 1922, and with 103,131,000 tons in 1921, or an increase in the two years of over 10 per cent in the physical quantity of the commodities transported.
The growth of lake transportation and of ocean transportation indicates correspondingly large increases in volume.
Then also in the matter of employment, had I time to go into it, I could point out wherein the Department of Labour index figures show very definite improvement in that regard.
As to public finance, the House has already a statement showing vastly reduced expenditure with vastly increased revenues, making the best showing which this country has known for a long period of time.
Then adding other indices of general business, such as bank clearings, stock figures,

securities and the like, one sees on every side the indication of a growing and increasing prosperity. There, Mr. Speaker, is the best answer to all that we have been obliged to listen to in the way of detraction on the part of my right hon. friend as to the condition ' of the country, its general business and its finances. That is the answer which we, as a government, make to the criticisms which our friends opposite have directed towards us ; it is what we give to the country in account of our stewardship of the nation's affairs.
In conclusion, Sir, we believe the time has come when, instead of sounding a note of pessimism, we are justified in giving to the country a note of optimism. More than that, we feel the time has come when, instead of making appeals of a sectional character to interests in the east or to interests in the west, we ought to address ourselves rather to the nation as a whole. My right hon. friend and I had the privilege of hearing the other day an address, delivered by Mr. Vincent Massey-one of the young men of this country, accustomed to observe matters carefully and in an impartial way. He was speaking to the citizens of Ottawa, and equally to the people of Canada. He said, "It is not Downing Street but Main Street which is the foe of true Canadianism." The newspaper report of this speech contains the following:
Turning to his theme, the speaker said the whole air seemed charged with the problematical, but so far as he was concerned he would prefer to emphasize the word Canadian rather than problems. He criticized a sectional outlook which he thought was discernible. . . But he had not much sympathy with those who saw b'ue ruin, red revolution, and a yellow peril, a sort of Joseph's coat of misery, which he thought also was hardly the best kind of flag under which to move towards better things.
That expression of view given at a Canadian Club meeting by Mr. Vincent Massey is, I think, the voice of the younger generation of Canada to-day of those who have faith in the country and want to see it go forward, of those who do not approve of the continual note of detraction, of pessimism and of sectionalism which has been sounded so much of late by my right hon. friend and his friends. I have spoken of the young men, let me give my hon. friend the words of an old man, one of the grand old men of this country, one most highly honoured and revered, one who some years ago used to sit in this House as a Conservative member. I give him the words oT Mr. Adam Brown, of Hamilton, now in his ninety-eighth year, words which sound a note of optimism more emphatic than those already quoted and which he and his associates might well take to heart and repeat to the country

as often as they can, for they are uttered by one who has been a keen observer of Canadian affairs for three quarters of a century. Concluding an address to the staff of the Canada Life Assurance Company last month, when for the fourtieth time he moved the vote of thanks to them for their services, Mr. Brown said:
No country in the world begins the new year with greater assurance of prosperity than Canada. Let us as Canadians be prouder than ever of our great inheritance, full of hope and faith in the future that awaits our beloved Canada-a land of peace and plenty, welded heart and soul to the greatest and freest empire the world has ever known, and with hearts that change not, resolve that we will be true to our trust, rendering honest and noble service to our country whatever our calling in it may be, and handing down unsullied to millions yet unborn the precious and priceless blessings we enjoy as British subjects, under the unstained flag of our fathers.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the faith, this the spirit needed to make our country great.

Baker Memorial

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Your Excellency, Ladies and Gentlemen: On the morrow of the eventful election of 1911, late in the autumn, parliament was convened at this very spot, under the" gothic arches of the old building which soon after was to crumble and become but a memory. Amongst the new commoners appeared a young man of middle stature with an attractive expression of youth and strength combined. An early training of self-discipline and an exuberance of life blended into a harmonious whole made of him a winning personality full of vitality and charm. He hailed from the Eastern Townships, a picturesque country of rolling hills, dotted with sheets of placid and clear waters, where a luxuriant nature seems to fashion in her bosom the sterling character of her sons.
Harold Baker came from good lineage. His father long before him had, on the forum and in the legislative halls of Quebec and Ottawa, served faithfully and eloquently his country. The son had just gallantly wrested from a loyal and deserving public servant after a momentous battle, the coveted prize of his ambition.
The mandate of Brome was his and in his new career, like that of his forbears, he meant to devote many years of service to the public weal.
Three sessions passed. The House of Commons, busily engaged in enacting laws and solving problems, was hardly keeping pace with the ever-expanding forces of a young and progressive Dominion.
When all of a sudden, in the midst of a glorious summer, the first rumblings of a terrific storm were heard at a distance. From across the Atlantic, threatening lights were seen on the horizon and as hours and minutes fled, the impending storm had gathered and was soon raging from Halifax to Victoria.
The great World War was on us with its long and sombre periods of supreme trials, of hopes deferred, with its unending trail of holocausts on land, in the air and on the seas.
The youngest member of the House of Commons, Harold Baker, was one of the first to answer the call of duty. He saw that duty clearly before him and we, his colleagues, can well remember with what a radiant faith he joined the colours and bade us adieu.
As weeks and months elapsed, the yeomen gathered from the deepest recesses of this broad Dominion and the steady tramp of regiments began, as if marching in rhythmical order, with the roll of the drums. With unfaltering steps, the sun glinting on their bayonets, the first contingents reached Valcartier, impatient to board the Argosies bound for the battlefields of France all ablaze in the deadliest conflict ever witnessed between right and might.
Theirs was not a spectacular adventure. Modern warfare has lost that glamour which in centuries past stirred the imagination of peoples. When whole nations are aligned on the battlefields in a long maze of muddy burrows, war becomes anonymous. Officers and privates face the same dangers, they share the same fate. And so, in June, 1916, a brief and melancholy despatch brought us face to face with the grim and poignant realties of war. Lt.-Col. Harold Baker, our fellow member, had been killed in action at Sanctuary Wood.
The parliament of Canada, shocked, aggrieved at the sad message, felt deeply honoured at the noble example of manhood set by its Benjamin, and unanimously it resolved that another sanctuary, within its own precincts, would be dedicated to him, so that his memory would ever be enshrined with those laurels which since ancient times are the happy warrior's halo.
It is proper and fitting that Your Excellency, you who so gloriously led our Canadian boys to victory in one of the most strategic and decisive engagements of the long and bloody struggle, should be called upon to unveil this, the first monument erected in our Hall of Fame.
This bronze memorial is not only the artistic expression of the gratitiude of the nation to one dearly beloved. It is also a pious memento to all those young Canadians who, during four years of cruel agony, so prized liberty that to save it no sacrifice was for them too great.
It will stand here, at the threshold of the House of Commons, for all time to come, as a supreme lesson of the dead to the living- that love of country, devotion to duty, are not empty words or vain ideals.
It will vividly recall to future generations that the dropping volleys and the muffled drums signalling there yonder the sacrifice of so, many precious lives, was also meant as a supplication to the world that hereafter the gigantic evil of war should be stopped before it got afoot.
Let that ideal for which our heroes laid down their lives be forever our guiding star. Then can it be said that from their exhausted frame buried in distant fields, their soul still radiates in our land-consoling the ones, stimu-
Baker Memorial..

lating the others-a soul refulgent with that spirit of human brotherhood which two thousand years ago was heralded in the plains of Judea by the messengers of the Prince of Peace.
Then, and then only, will it be proclaimed that Canada, bereaved by the loss of her bravest, hath through their sacrifice gained in spiritualities; that as they dashed fearlessly into the fiery furnace they bequeathed to us, the living, a noble and lasting inspiration with a memory emerging from the perishable to immortality.
His Excellency the Governor General unveiled the monument, the guard presenting arms and the bugler sounding The Last Post.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING, C.M.G., P.C., (Prime Minister): Mr. Chairman, Your Excellency, Ladies and Gentlemen: The ceremony in which we are participators to-day is one of historic as well as personal interest to all present. It is very fitting that the first monument to be unveiled in these halls of parliament as reconstructed since the Great War, should be to the memory of a distinguished member of the Canadian House of Commons who was hilled in action. It is scarcely less significant, and will indeed be deeply gratifying to all Canadians, that the unveiling of the memorial should be by His Excellency, Lord Byng, who was in command of the Canadian Corps during the action in which Colonel Baker fell, and who to-day is our Governor General.
We are proud that parliament has seen well to pay this tribute to the memory of [DOT]one of her gallant sons, but we would greatly err if this memorial did not speak to us of something more than individual loss and individual sacrifice. It is personal in character, but it is also essentially symbolic. It speaks not of one member of parliament only who gallantly served his country overseas, but of the fifty or more members of the two Houses who enlisted at the time, many of whom served actively in France, and of the eighteen members of parliament who lost sons in the Great War. But it speaks of more than this. It speaks of Canadians, approximately 600,000 in number who enlisted for service in the Great War, and above all of the more than 60,000 who gave their lives as the supreme sacrifice of this nation in the cause of the World's freedom. Of-one and all of these it can be said,
, as it was said of the late Colonel Baker in the legend that appears to the left of the bronze figure:	"And thus this man died, leaving
his death for an example of a noble courage, and a memorial of virtue, not only unto young men but unto all his Nation."
The wider association and larger significance of the memorial is emphasized by 'the words of the legend which appears to the right of the figure. To appreciate them in all their impressiveness' we must recall that they were written by another distinguished Canadian who died of wounds received in the Great War, and whose remains lie, like those of Colonel Baker, in one of the military cemeteries overseas:
To you from falling hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high.
If ye break faith with us who die,
We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders fields.
The legend to the left is our tribute to the immortal dead. The legend to the right is their command to us. The legend to the left comes to us out of the distant past, recalling that great company of the defenders of right and of the faith, who through the ages have revealed the God-like greatness of the human spirit and have entered into the fulness of eternal life. The words of the legend to the right will continue to speak to us through all the years that lie ahead, reminding us of the obligations we who are living owe to those who are gone and to whom in the words of another poet we said: Here-or hereafter-you shall see it ended,
This mighty work to which your souls are set;
If from beyond-then, whit the vision splendid,
You shall smile back and never know regret.
Pray God we may be given strength and grace and guidance to be true to this greatest of all trusts.
Lastly, may I say that it will always be a source of pride and satisfaction to all who view this splendid work of art to know that it also is the creation of another distinguished Canadian, Dr. Tait McKenzie, who, though at present residing in the United States, was born in the near vicinity of Ottawa, and has remained a British subject. The excellence of Dr. McKenzie's art is recognized the world over, and we are proud that we should have this splendid bronze protrait of his as the first memorial to be unveiled in our parliamentary halls.
In a word, to-day's ceremonial is a noble expression of the many sidedness, of our national life-worthy in what in art it has revealed of sculpture and of verse, great in its parliamentary traditions and military achievements, but noblest in all in the manifestations of the spirit of our manhood, a spirit that is ever ready for service, and that falters not at sacrifice.

Baker Memorial
Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN P.C. (Leader of the Opposition): The event of this afternoon is the first of its kind in our country's history. It has been the lot of other nations to have their legislators, their parliamentarians, even their kings put on the uniform of soldiers and go forth to battle and meet a patriot's death, but so far it has been the lot of Canada only once. George Harry Baker, a gifted, comely, companionable man; the youngest of the members of the House of Commons, the centre of the hopes of his associates in parliament, the trusted of everyone, the choice of a fine old constituency, the pride of an honoured family, heard the solemn call of duty at the outbreak of the great war-he answered and he gave his life.
Thousands went to battle with him and thousands died, but Colonel Baker left a scene probably more dear to the ambitions, more attractive to aspiring manhood, than any from which others tore themselves away. There were others in the parliament of that day who joined the colors and went too. Some of them are with us still and all of them have an honoured place in memory and in public regard. But Colonel Baker alone never returned. He made the final sacrifice; bequeathed to his country the heritage of a great example and left for the records of this parliament the legacy of his gallant name.
The character of Colonel Baker is reflected, perhaps best of all, in the letters he wrote home and back to Canada during his service overseas. These are embalmed in a private biography published by his friends, and will be treasured by all who honour his memory. They disclose a modesty of demeanor, a cheerfulness of temperament, a human kindliness and with a splendid courage; qualities every one that we well knew he possessed. "I make no profession as a soldier" he said at a banquet in his honour prior to his departure, "I lay no claim to special merit. My aim is to win the confidence of my men and to leave the rest to circumstances and the turn of events." The confidence of his men he won, a confidence which reached a degree of ardor and devotion rarely equalled in our military annals. The story of the struggle in which he lost his life is one of the most tragic and thrilling in all the long and ghastly but glorious history of war. For a day and a night it raged and on into the next a thundering, deafening, murderous struggle-a struggle perhaps more distinctly Canadian on the allied side than any previous engagement. The names of Maple Copse, Observatory Ridge, and Armagh Wood, places where the sanguinary contest was waged should 4
be names forever remembered by the children of our Dominion. Companies went forward and bravely battled on after their arms had all but disappeared, many of their men deafened and blind, but discipline maintained to the end. General Griesbach, one of our Senators was there; General Macdonell, now Principal of Royal Military College at Kingston arrived also with his men on the scene, and General Draper whom we rejoice to see with us to-day-he too played a noble part. The figure of Harry Baker moving from point to point, making his dispositions for defence, cheering his men, encouraging them by his enthusiasm and his example, is the last memory which his batallion cherishes of their commanding officer. Brave to the last, smiling to the end, imperturbable, unselfish, full of cheer, a leader even in death, he illustrated how a soldier should battle and how gentlemen should die.
A brilliant career was cut short in its prime. All that man had to live for he left behind. A domestic felicity as sweet as ever enshrouded a life, he sacrificed; social position was his, this he sacrificed as well; a professional career already prosperous, this he abandoned, a public service splendid with promise, this too he left behind. The best that life had to offer he cheerfully surrendered that his whole duty might ba done.
We are accustomed to regard such an early ending of a splendid young man as the lamentable close of a life of promise. But the story of Harry Baker is a story of achievements won, even more than it is a story of promise lost. His years of maturity were crowded with things done and well done, in private life, in professional life, in public life, and on the field of war. It is in the spirit of such a career more than in expansion of territory, or even in continuance of Empire, that there lies the imperishable glory of the British name. The names of our great men, spread over the centuries, treasured forever by our children, the light that shines for their example; these are remembered and have their eternal value long after the events through which they passed have been forgotten. In the wide circle of his friends, in the larger area of his activities and his influence in the Eastern Townships where he was reared and which he loved, in the Dominion which he served, and for whose honour he died, Harold Baker will be known as one of those men.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT FORKE (Brandon, Leader of the Progressive Party):
speechtext:
I feel almost unworthy to take part in this ceremony, as I was not privileged to have the acquaintance of the one whose memory we

Baker Memorial

would honour this day. It is well as it is fitting that ceremonies such as this should take place; that monuments should be erected to the glorious dead. As the years roll away and time passes, time with healing influence will soften the blow that fell so heavily upon many, when the Great War was taking its heavy toll of human life. To them this will ever remain-the memory of the great loss sustained. But others,-and it is the way of humanity,-the incidents of those trying years will only be a memory. Maybe in the pressing importance of everyday duty they may forget the great sacrifice made by our glorious dead; and it is seemly that ceremonies such as this take place, that Memorial services be held, Memorial Halls built, Tablets set up and Monuments erected-Lest we forget! Lest we forget!
It is well that a monument should be erected in this building where one whose memory we honour served his country by representing his constituency in parliament. I was not personally acquainted with this fine soldier and gentleman, but enough for me, he heard the call of his country, he did his duty and failed not.
This statue shall stand to-day and in days to come as a constant reminder of one who did his duty and made the supreme sacrifice. It will be an inspiration to members of this House to serve their country to the best of t'heir ability, with singleness of purpose doing the duty that lies nearest to them. There will be differences of opinion, but let it be honest differences.
The story of the sacrifices our heroic dead made for liberty, for their country, will be forever one of the splendid pages in the history of Canada, and a glorious heritage for our children and our children's children, an inspiration to all who follow that they shall be worthy of the sacrifices made^ "Greater love hath no man than this that he lay down his life for his fellow men."
Hon. Sir JAMES LOUGHEED K.C.M.G., (Leader of the Opposition in the Senate): It is with mingled feelings of sorrow and pride that to-day we pay this tribute to Lieut.-Col. Baker who for some years was associated with us in the parliament of Canada.
In the prime of his manhood, when life was clothed with its greatest attractiveness and promise, he heard the tocsin of war-the . call of duty. All else was laid to one side and he responded with haste to the call of his country. He fell as a soldier and a fighting man would want to fall. He fell on the field of battle. In that world's conflict and clash of arms, the millions who died that we might have

liberty, will live on through the ages. Their deeds are immortal, and while we shall die and be forgotten, they shall always be our survivors.
In this monument of stone and bronze erected by a grateful country, Colonel Baker will outlive not only those living to-day who sat with him in the Parliament of Canada, but this record of his gallantry and death, his life and his sacrifice, will pass down to our descendants as an outstanding and inspiring memory in the history of the Canadian parliament.
While we mourn his death, yet it is with patriotic pride that we think how gallantly he fell. When from time to time in these stately halls we view this monument commemorative of his death, we shall ask ourselves:
And how can man die better
Than facing fearful odds,
For the ashes of his fathers,
And the temples of his Gods?
Hon. Senator GEO. G. FOSTER, K.C, (Alma):	Your Excellency, Mr. Chairman,
Ladies and Gentlemen:	From the hillside
and valleys, from the villages and home lands of that beautiful district in the Eastern Townships in which Harry Baker was bom, in which he lived his life, in which his heart was centered and from whence he marched to glory, I have been asked by his neighbours, as one of their sons, to bring a message of gratitude and appreciation on this dedication day to the members of the Senate and of the House of Commons.
It is not only because you have written in stone and bronze the features and story of the sacrifice of our hero; it is not only because you have added to the glory of the traditions of your parliament by preserving the details of his service, but it is because we know that without a dissenting voice two parliaments have unanimously joined in this noble tribute, and you have thereby spread his fame throughout our country by linking it with this magnifieient structure. For all these reasons, our people are truly grateful.
I am quite certain that I am within the mandate entrusted to me and am voicing their wishes when I express to the four leaders of political thought, who have so generously honoured his memory, the gratitude that will be felt for them; and I can say that there will be written into the history of those Eastern Counties a true transcript of the patriotic lessons which may be learned from their utterances, and they will serve as an incentive for present and future generations to emulate the example of the hero of to-day, not only in case the country may demand a similar service, but in those other walks of life in which

I am not going to attempt to add one word to what has been said of the history and sacrifice which has been referred to, but only to express the hope that as day by day we pass within the shadow of the monument we have erected we may remember the service which Colonel Baker rendered to Canada, at a time of great national peril, and that we, too, may emulate his example in our everyday service.
